prompt:
A student claims: 'Taking ten repeated measurements and calculating their mean will eliminate all experimental errors.'
Explain why this claim is incorrect with reference to:
(i) random errors, [1]
(ii) systematic errors. [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: Part (i): Averaging reduces the effect of random errors (as deviations cancel), but does not completely eliminate them.
Part (ii): Averaging does not remove systematic errors because all readings share the same directional offset, which remains in the mean.

hints: Does averaging completely eliminate random fluctuations or just reduce their effect?
If every single reading is 2 mm too high, what is the average?
solution: (i) Averaging reduces the effect of random errors because positive and negative deviations partly cancel, but it does not eliminate them entirely. (ii) Averaging has no effect on systematic errors because every measurement is shifted in the same direction, so the mean contains the exact same offset.
teacher_walkthrough: (i) Random errors: independent repeats allow positive and negative fluctuations to cancel partially, reducing their effect, but finite repeats never guarantee zero random error.
(ii) Systematic errors: because every reading is biased in the same direction by the same cause (e.g. zero error), their mean carries the identical bias. Repetition cannot remove a systematic error.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored drill clarifying why repetition reduces random errors but leaves systematic errors intact.
